not_claimed: Any DHS-published processing time for an ALR or PCH license — no rule-stated days-to-license was found. Only the pre-licensure inspection requirement and the 3-month post-licensure reinspection are verified.

The current adjusted ALR per-bed fee — only the $75 base in 55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800 is verified, and it was adjusted by a 2018 Pennsylvania Bulletin notice (48 Pa.B. 3493) whose amount was not retrieved. The PCH fee tiers come from the regulation as reproduced by Cornell LII; DHS's own application page lists a different smallest tier (4–20 beds), and the regulation was used.

Exactly when the initial ALR fee is paid — the DHS notice (secondary relay) says the check goes in with the application packet, while the regulation text ties the fees to issuance or renewal. Confirm with BHSL before paying.

Contract rates for licensed-nurse coverage. The requirement itself is verified (a licensed nurse available in the building or on call at all times, §2800.60(d)), but the $800/$2,000/$6,000 monthly lines are operator estimates and have not been tested against 24/7 coverage plus assessments and quarterly plan reviews.

ALR minimum staff-to-resident ratios beyond the verified rules (one 21+ direct care staff person present whenever residents are present; 1 hour/day per mobile resident; 1 CPR/first-aid-trained person per 35 residents). A secondary claim of 1:8 awake and 1:18 asleep conflicts with older summaries and was not used.

Prices for the 100-hour administrator course, the 18-hour direct care pre-service training, CPR/first-aid certification and the dementia training (4 hours within 30 days, 2 hours annually). The hour requirements are verified (§2800.64, .65, .69), but the costs are operator estimates.

Zoning, certificate-of-occupancy process and fees, and State Fire Marshal floor-plan approval process and fees — no official DHS or municipal source was retrieved. Written fire safety approval before licensure and a certificate of occupancy check are verified rules; the secondary Flaney Capital claim of proof of zoning approval is not confirmed.

Liability, professional, auto or bond insurance minimums for ALR or PCH licensure — none found. Workers' compensation is mandatory for any employer with employees, but the PCRB class code for assisted living and the 4% payroll rate are unverified.

OLTL/CHC per-unit rates and procedure codes for personal care services in ALR/PCH settings — the OLTL HCBS rate files dated January 1 and July 1, 2026 are listed by DHS but were not retrieved, and the W1793 amount was not verified as current.

Community HealthChoices managed care organization contract rates, provider contract terms, whether CHC pays any ALR or PCH residence charge, and PA-specific provider enrollment steps and fees. DHS states PCHs and ALRs are typically not covered by Medicaid and rates are set by the facility. Whether the federal CY2026 $750 enrollment fee applies to a PCH or ALR operator was not confirmed.
Whether the July 1, 2026 CHC 1915(c) waiver amendment took effect, and the official CHC waitlist counts or wait times.

The state PCH supplement for ALR residents. The $85 personal needs allowance (§2600.25a) and the $639.30 PCH supplement are verified for personal care homes. Whether SSI-level ALR residents receive the supplement is unverified, so the SSI resident payment in the rates table is a model calculation.

Official statewide counts of licensed PCHs and ALRs, occupancy or vacancy rates, referral-source mix, market shares and competitor names — DHS gives only 'more than 1,000' BHSL-licensed congregate settings of all types and about 40,000 adults served. The 994 PCH figure is from an unverified third-party directory and is not used.

A single official private-pay price for Pennsylvania assisted living — Genworth 2024 ($73,206/yr), CareScout 2025 via a secondary guide ($77,760/yr) and A Place for Mom ($5,655/mo) differ, and other figures with unknown methodology were excluded. All measure assisted living communities, not small personal care homes.

A single authoritative 65+ population figure for the latest vintage — the Department of Aging gives more than 2.5 million (2020 Census), USAFacts about 2.67 million (2024) and a news report about 2.8 million (2026 estimates).

May 2025 OEWS Pennsylvania wages for RNs, LPNs, cooks and administrators at the state level, and Philadelphia metro wages — not retrieved. Only the PA nursing assistant median and the Pittsburgh management group mean were found. The $7.25 minimum wage rests on secondary sources, not the Department of Labor & Industry page.

A statewide minimum wage above $7.25 — a $15 bill passed the House but is not enacted, and the Senate blocked a forcing vote. Philadelphia and Pittsburgh cannot set local minimum wages for private employers (secondary source).
Municipal earned income tax rates and Pittsburgh local wage tax; the 2026 new-employer UC rate (3.822%) is secondary-sourced only.

Entity formation fees ($125 LLC, $7 annual report, $250 foreign registration) were taken from secondary sources, not the Department of State fee schedule. Sources conflict on the annual report due date, and September 30 was used.

Commercial rent for assisted living or care-facility space, and HUD FY2027 Fair Market Rents (effective Oct 1, 2026). Only HUD FY2026 FMRs (Philadelphia and Pittsburgh) are available as a residential rent benchmark.

Pending 2026 rulemaking amending Chapter 2600 or 2800 — none found, and the online Pa. Code is current only through the Pennsylvania Bulletin date shown on the site. ALR waiver-of-regulation requests open for the 30-day comment period were not retrieved.
BHSL headquarters address and phone — the pa.gov contact page and a field-office page conflict; confirm before publishing.
Quote caveat: most quotes were taken from search-result excerpts, not full-page fetches; re-verify against live pages before publication.

Prices for a contracted dietitian, an accessible vehicle with driver labor, unit-level plant upgrades (private bathrooms, call systems, thermostats, central A/C, AED, public restroom), fire safety renewals and water testing. Each is a required item, and none is verified or fully priced in the model.

Wage figures that could not be re-verified from primary pages: the CareScout 2025 $6,480/month (via LTCareNav), the A Place for Mom $5,655/month, and the Pittsburgh management mean of $61.57/hr. Confirm each against the primary table or PDF before relying on it.

occupancy.rationale: No Pennsylvania-specific PCH/ALR occupancy or vacancy figure was found in official sources (see not_claimed). The 88% default, 80% conservative and 95% optimistic cases are operator planning assumptions, not sourced rates. S19 supports only the context that homes range from 4 to several hundred residents and that charges are facility-set. Small homes swing more because one vacancy is a large share of census: 1 of 6 beds is about 17%, 1 of 16 is about 6%, 1 of 40 is 2.5%. New residences ramp up from the first admission after DHS licensure.

configurations.label: 6-bed small residence (converted house), 100% private pay
configurations.notes: Smallest practical model. Chapter 2800 applies to four or more unrelated adults served for more than 24 hours [S5], and homes may be licensed for as few as four residents [S19]. Staffing is modeled on the verified ALR rules in Chapter 2800: a direct care staff person age 21+ present whenever residents are present, and at least 1 hour/day of assisted living service per mobile resident [S3][S5]. PCH staffing rules under Chapter 2600 were not retrieved, so a 6-bed home licensed as a PCH may differ. Price is the lowest of the three public benchmarks ($5,655/mo, A Place for Mom) [S33] because Genworth/CareScout measure a private one-bedroom in an assisted living community [S31][S32], not a small residential home. Model result: this configuration loses money at the sourced price. 24-hour coverage at the PA nursing assistant median wage costs more than six residents pay, unless the owner personally fills care shifts. The administrator line is the owner's pay. Philadelphia-area HUD rents are about 30% higher than the Pittsburgh figures used here [S49].

staffing.role: Direct care staff, one person 21+ present 24/7 (730 hrs/month)
staffing.cite: 55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800 (direct care staff person 21+ present whenever residents are present)
staffing.notes: Rule requires a direct care staff person age 21+ in the residence at all times one or more residents are present [S3]. Staff on duty must be awake at all times (§2800.58), so no sleep-shift discount applies. Wage is the Pennsylvania nursing assistant median, $21.44/hr ($44,590/yr), BLS OEWS May 2025 via O*NET [S35]. It is above the $7.25 state minimum wage [S38]. A $15 minimum wage bill passed the House but is not enacted [S39][S40]. Philadelphia and Pittsburgh cannot set higher local minimums for private employers [S41]. Food service, housekeeping and laundry (weekly linen change) are mandatory and staffing must cover them (§2800.60(c)). This configuration has no separate cook/housekeeping/laundry line, so the 730 direct-care hours plus the service-time line are assumed to absorb that work. If separate staff are hired, cost rises.

staffing.role: Assisted living service time (1 hr/day per mobile resident = 30.42 hrs per resident-month)
staffing.cite: 55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800 (1 hr/day per mobile resident; 75% in waking hours)
staffing.notes: Rule-derived: direct care staff must be available to provide at least 1 hour/day of assisted living services to each mobile resident (2 hrs/day for residents with mobility needs), with at least 75% in waking hours [S5]. Modeled as additional hours on top of the 24/7 presence coverage, which is conservative because the on-shift person also provides some of this time. The model assumes mobile residents; at 2 hrs/day this line doubles.

staffing.role: Administrator (owner-operator; on site an average 36+ hrs/week in each calendar month)
staffing.notes: Operator estimate — verify locally. Administrator-specific Pennsylvania wage data was not retrieved. The only wage reference found is the Pittsburgh MSA management group mean of $61.57/hr (about $128,066/yr), BLS May 2025, which covers all management occupations and is a ceiling reference only [S37]. At that salary this configuration's monthly result would fall by about $7,200 more. If the owner serves as administrator, this line is the owner's pay. Qualification paths include an RN license plus 1 year of experience in the prior 10 years [S5]. Required on-site presence: average 36+ hrs/week per calendar month [S3]. Annual training must come from Department-approved sources [S13].

configurations.label: 16-bed assisted living residence, 100% private pay
configurations.notes: Mid-size residence in a purpose-built or converted building with one unit per resident. Price is the Genworth 2024 Pennsylvania median of $73,206/yr ($6,100.50/mo) for a private one-bedroom in an assisted living community [S31], which fits a unit-based building better than a shared-room home. The CareScout 2025 figure of $6,480/mo is higher but only secondary-sourced [S32], and A Place for Mom shows $5,655/mo [S33]. Roughly break-even near 80% occupancy and marginal above it. New-construction single-resident units must be at least 225 sq ft; pre-2011 facilities have a 160 sq ft rule [S3]. The CPR/first-aid requirement is one trained person per 35 residents [S3], so one is enough at 16 residents.

configurations.notes: Shows the effect of accepting SSI-level residents. Pennsylvania has no assisted-living Medicaid waiver [S22], DHS says PCH/ALR charges are typically not covered by Medicaid and are facility-set [S19], and Community HealthChoices does not pay residence charges as far as this research could verify [S18]. An SSI-level resident is modeled as contributing the 2026 SSI plus state supplement for a personal care boarding home ($1,633.30, SSA) minus the $85 personal needs allowance = $1,548.30/month [S21][S23]. The $85 allowance is verified for personal care homes (§2600.25a), and ALR charges are capped at the SSI resident's income minus the personal needs allowance (§2800.27(a)). However, the $639.30 supplement is verified only for residents of licensed personal care homes. Whether it applies to ALR residents is unverified; confirm with BHSL/SSA. Dual-licensed PCH/ALR operation is the clearer path (§2800.11(g)). This is a modeled figure, and DHS does not require a facility to accept it as payment in full. SSI residents must receive hygiene items, laundry and ADL/IADL assistance at no charge beyond that amount (§2800.27(d)); that cost is not modeled. Same building and staff as the private-pay 16-bed model.

sections.executive_summary:
Pennsylvania licenses two overlapping kinds of residential senior care, and both fall under the same regulator. The **Assisted Living Residence (ALR)** is governed by 55 Pa. Code Chapter 2800. The **Personal Care Home (PCH)** is governed by a separate chapter, 55 Pa. Code Chapter 2600 [S3][S4][S20]. DHS's Office of Long-Term Living (OLTL), through its Bureau of Human Services Licensing (BHSL), is responsible for licensing both [S1][S2][S50]. Both license types cover premises serving four or more adults who are not relatives of the operator, for more than 24 hours [S4][S5]. DHS reports that homes may be licensed for as few as four residents and as many as several hundred [S19].

Money comes almost entirely from residents and families. DHS says the vast majority of PCH and ALR residents pay privately, and that PCHs and ALRs are typically not covered by Medicaid, with payment rates set by the facility [S19]. A secondary source reports that Pennsylvania has no assisted-living Medicaid waiver [S22]. Some residents also receive Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) [S19]. Those flow through Community HealthChoices (CHC), OLTL's mandatory managed long-term services and supports program [S18][S26]. A lower-income resident can instead pay the facility the SSI-plus-state-supplement amount. SSA lists $1,633.30/month for an eligible individual in a personal care boarding home in 2026 [S21]. The modeled contribution after an $85 personal needs allowance is $1,548.30 [S21][S23]. The $85 allowance and the $639.30 supplement are verified for personal care homes; whether the supplement applies to ALR residents is unverified.

The private-pay benchmark is the Genworth 2024 Pennsylvania median of $73,206/yr (about $6,100/month) for a private one-bedroom in an assisted living community [S31]. The 2025 CareScout figure of $6,480/month (secondary citation) is higher [S32]. A Place for Mom's $5,655/month is lower [S33]. None of these measures a shared room in a small residential home.

**Bottom line from the model.** At 88% occupancy, three of the five configurations are profitable and two lose money. The 40-unit private-pay residence nets about $24,335/month (11.3% margin), breaks even at about 74.7% occupancy, first turns profitable in month 11, and needs about $1.25 million of cash. The 16-bed private-pay residence nets about $5,541/month (6.5%), breaks even at about 80.4% occupancy, and needs about $392,000. The 40-unit residence with 15% SSI-level residents nets only about $299/month and needs about 87.8% occupancy to break even. The 6-bed private-pay house loses about $7,630/month and cannot break even even at full occupancy. The 16-bed residence with 25% SSI-level residents loses about $10,483/month. The model finds no profit in a small house staffed by paid labor, and none in an SSI-heavy mix at the benchmark price. These results do not include a priced dietitian contract, a fully costed accessible transportation service, the 100-hour administrator course, or unit-level plant upgrades, so actual results will be lower.

### What this report does not claim
- Any DHS-published licensing processing time, or the current adjusted per-bed fee (the $75 base predates a 2018 adjustment notice).
- CHC or OLTL per-unit rates for services in ALR/PCH settings, or any CHC payment of residence charges.
- Statewide occupancy, competitor names, market shares, or official counts of PCHs versus ALRs.
- Zoning, certificate-of-occupancy, State Fire Marshal or insurance requirements and costs.
- Chapter 2600 (PCH) staffing rules. The financial model applies the verified Chapter 2800 rules.
- Prices for a dietitian contract, the 100-hour administrator course, accessible transportation and unit-level plant upgrades.
sections.service_model:
**Who is served.** Chapter 2800 frames assisted living residences as a long-term care alternative that lets people age in place [S5]. An ALR serves four or more unrelated adults for more than 24 hours [S5]. DHS says BHSL serves about 40,000 adults with a wide variety of care needs across all the settings it licenses, including people with intellectual and developmental disabilities [S2]. DHS does not split that figure between ALR and PCH residents.

**Two license types.** An ALR is licensed under 55 Pa. Code Chapter 2800. Created by Act 56 of 2007, its regulations took effect in January 2011 (secondary source) [S22]. The Department adopted Chapter 2800 by final-form rulemaking published July 17, 2010 [S59]. A PCH is licensed under Chapter 2600. Chapter 2800 states that it does not apply to personal care homes, domiciliary care homes, independent living communities or commercial boarding homes [S20]. A secondary market guide says Pennsylvania has far more PCHs than ALRs, with no count given [S22]. This research found no verified official count of either type.

**Regulator.** Official DHS pages state that OLTL's Bureau of Human Services Licensing is responsible for licensure and regulatory compliance of both PCHs and ALRs [S1][S2][S50]. One secondary source describes a split between BHSL and OLTL, which conflicts with the official pages. This report follows the official pages.

**Service model that the financial model prices.** The model follows the verified Chapter 2800 rules:
- A direct care staff person age 21 or older must be in the residence whenever one or more residents are present [S3].
- Direct care staff must be available to provide at least 1 hour/day of assisted living services to each mobile resident (2 hours/day for residents with mobility needs), with at least 75% of those hours during waking hours [S5].
- Single-resident living units in new construction must be at least 225 square feet. Pre-2011 facilities have a 160 sq ft rule [S3].
- Resident contracts must identify the core service package and its total price [S3].
- Capacity is fixed on the license, and an increase needs prior DHS approval before more residents are admitted [S3].

**What is not modeled.** The model does not use Chapter 2600 staffing or physical-plant rules, so a home licensed as a PCH may have different staffing and cost. It also does not cover dementia-specific programming. Operators choosing between a PCH and an ALR license should read both chapters in full [S3][S4].
sections.licensing_pathway:
**Regulatory currency.** The official Pennsylvania Code site states it reflects changes effective through 56 Pa.B. 5370 (August 8, 2026) [S51]. No pending 2026 rulemaking amending Chapter 2600 or 2800 was found, but check the Pennsylvania Bulletin before filing.

**Step-by-step (ALR).**
1. **Form the entity.** A domestic LLC Certificate of Organization costs $125 one time, and the LLC annual report is $7 due September 30 under Act 122 of 2022 (both secondary-sourced) [S46][S47]. Pennsylvania has no LLC franchise tax, and members pay the flat 3.07% personal income tax on pass-through income (secondary) [S47].
2. **Secure the building and approvals.** The pre-licensure package must include a floor plan showing all floors and every internal and external exit path [S11]. Inspectors verify that the residence has a new or modified certificate of occupancy before any change in building use [S12]. Written fire safety approval is required before a license is issued and must be renewed at least every 3 years [S3]. Local zoning rules and State Fire Marshal floor-plan fees were not verified. A secondary guide mentions proof of zoning approval, which is not confirmed against an official DHS list.
3. **Qualify the administrator and run clearances.** The DHS review list requires administrator education and training documentation and criminal history checks for the owner/operator under the Older Adult Protective Services Act [S11][S15]. Before initial employment the administrator must complete a Department-approved orientation, a 100-hour standardized Department-approved training course and a competency test with a passing score (§2800.64). One qualifying administrator path is an RN license plus 1 year of direct care or administrative experience in the prior 10 years. Other paths include LPN and nursing home administrator licenses [S5]. Owners or operators who are not Pennsylvania residents and will work in the residence must also provide an FBI background check [S11].
4. **File the pre-licensure package.** Documents go to BHSL headquarters before the initial inspection [S10]. BHSL contact is 717-783-3670 and ra-pwarlheadquarters@pa.gov, at 555 Walnut Street, Forum Place 6th Floor, Harrisburg, PA 17101. The Operator Support Hotline is (866) 503-3926, open 9 a.m.–4 p.m. each Commonwealth business day [S17]. The illegal-operation/complaint line is 1-877-401-8835. A field-office page lists a different address and phone, so confirm before use.
5. **Pass the initial inspection.** Before a residence is initially licensed and permitted to open, operate or admit residents, DHS inspects it (§2800.11(b)) [S6]. You cannot admit residents before this.
6. **Pay the fees.** The ALR application or renewal fee is $300, plus a per-bed fee. The regulation base is $75 per bed, and DHS adjusts it by Pennsylvania Bulletin notice [S3][S5]. A 2018 notice (48 Pa.B. 3493) adjusted it, so $75 is likely stale and the exact current amount is unverified. At the $75 base that is $750 for 6 beds, $1,500 for 16 and $3,300 for 40. **Timing is unresolved.** The regulation ties the fees to issuing or renewing the license [S3][S6], and DHS says the ALR per-bed fee is due before the renewal certificate issues [S7]. A relay of a DHS notice says a new application packet is mailed with the fee by check or money order payable to DHS [S8]. Confirm with BHSL before paying. The model also divides the fees by 12 as if renewal were annual, and the renewal cycle was not verified.
7. **Post-licensure.** DHS reinspects a newly licensed residence within 3 months of initial licensure [S6]. State law requires at least one annual unannounced onsite inspection of each PCH and ALR [S16], and DHS also investigates complaints and unusual incidents [S19].

**Timeline.** No rule-stated number of days from application to license was found, so none is claimed. Plan around the inspection sequence above and the building work, which is usually the longest item.

**Penalty for operating unlicensed.** Under §2800.262(g), a residence found operating without a license is assessed $500. An additional $20 per resident per day applies after 14 days if no application has been filed [S3].

**Requests for waiver of regulation.** DHS opens ALR waiver-of-regulation requests for a 30-day public comment period [S50]. The open list was not retrieved. Many categories cannot be waived: scope, staff training, fire safety, assessment/support plan/service delivery, contract requirements and resident rights (§2800.19(c)). A copy of the waiver request must be given to the affected resident at least 30 days before submission (§2800.19(d)).

**PCH alternative.** The PCH application fee is tiered by bed count: $15 for 0–20 beds, $20 for 21–50, $30 for 51–100 and $50 for 101 or more [S9]. A DHS application page lists a different smallest tier (4–20 beds), and the regulation text was used. DHS also reinspects new PCHs within 3 months [S60]. The rest of the Chapter 2600 pathway was not researched in this bundle.

**Medicaid is a separate step.** Licensure does not enroll you in any payer. Whether a PCH or ALR operator must pay the federal CY2026 $750 provider enrollment application fee [S30] was not confirmed for Pennsylvania.
sections.reimbursement:
**How money actually flows.** Pennsylvania is a private-pay market for both PCHs and ALRs. DHS states that PCHs and ALRs are typically not covered by Medicaid, that payment rates are set by the facility, and that the vast majority of residents pay privately, though some also receive HCBS [S19]. A secondary source attributes to DHS a statement that PCHs and ALRs generally receive no third-party reimbursement [S25], and another reports that Pennsylvania has no assisted-living Medicaid waiver [S22]. No official source on whether CHC pays any PCH or ALR residence charge was found. **The financial model therefore includes no Medicaid or CHC revenue.**

**Private pay.** Three benchmarks bracket the price:
- Genworth 2024: $73,206/yr, about $6,100.50/month, Pennsylvania median, private one-bedroom, up 10% from 2023, national rank 24 [S31]. This is the figure the model uses for unit-based buildings (16 and 40 units).
- CareScout 2025 via a secondary guide: $6,480/month ($77,760/yr) [S32].
- A Place for Mom proprietary data: $5,655/month [S33]. The model uses this lowest figure for the 6-bed converted house.

All three measure assisted living communities and none measures a shared room in a small home. Pennsylvania's nursing home semi-private median is $141,985/yr [S31], which is the alternative level of care families compare against.

**SSI and the state supplement.** SSA's 2026 Pennsylvania table lists $1,633.30/month for an eligible person in a personal care boarding home and $1,628.30 in domiciliary care [S21]. The federal 2026 individual rate is $994 [S24], and a secondary source splits the PCBH total as $994 plus a $639.30 state supplement [S23]. A secondary source describes the supplement as a state-funded SSI add-on for residents of licensed PCHs or ALRs, not a Medicaid payment [S22]. The same source says the resident pays the SSI-plus-supplement amount minus an $85 personal needs allowance (cited to 55 Pa. Code §2600.25a, not verified from DHS) [S23]. That gives **$1,548.30/month**, about a quarter of the Genworth benchmark price. A facility is not required to accept this as payment in full, since rates are facility-set [S19].

**Community HealthChoices (CHC).** OLTL runs managed long-term services and supports through CHC, a capitated Medicaid managed care program [S18]. It is described as mandatory for adults 21 and older [S26], and Medicaid long-term care payments pass through the managed care plans rather than directly from the state (secondary) [S26]. About 383,000 people were enrolled as of June 2024, with 34% receiving HCBS [S58]. The CHC waiver is listed on Medicaid.gov as approved, with an application dated June 26, 2026 [S53]. OLTL states the CHC re-procurement RFA is in a stay and that CHC will keep operating under the current managed care organizations until further notice [S52]. DHS sets HCBS reimbursement rates through an actuarial process and public comment [S27]. Its CY 2025 rate study reported OLTL rates about 8% below ODP rates on a weighted SFY 2021–2022 basis [S28]. DHS lists OLTL HCBS rate files effective January 1 and July 1, 2026 [S27], but the amounts were not retrieved. The 15-minute unit and code W1793 for agency personal assistance are listed [S28], but the dollar rate was not verified.

**EVV.** If you ever deliver Medicaid-funded personal care visits, DHS requires electronic visit verification for payment of those claims, effective July 1, 2020 [S29]. No Medicaid revenue is modeled, so no EVV cost is included.

**Not claimed.** CHC plan contract rates, whether CHC pays any ALR or PCH residence charge, and PA-specific provider enrollment steps and fees.
sections.demand:
**What can be verified.** Pennsylvania has a large and growing older population. The Department of Aging reports more than 2.5 million residents aged 65 and older in the 2020 Census [S54]. The Pennsylvania State Data Center reports that 20% of the population was 65 or older in 2023 and that the 65+ group added 184,773 people (+7.6%) between 2020 and 2023 [S55]. USAFacts puts the 2024 figure at about 2.67 million, or 20.4% of residents [S56]. These vintages differ and no single authoritative latest-vintage figure was confirmed.

**Supply signals.** DHS says BHSL oversees more than 1,000 congregate care settings of all licensed types and serves about 40,000 adults [S2]. That is not a PCH/ALR count. A secondary guide says Pennsylvania has far more PCH-licensed homes than ALR-licensed residences [S22]. A third-party directory lists 994 licensed PCHs, drawn from an open-data set and unconfirmed by DHS [S57], so it is not used in any calculation. Licensed homes range from 4 to several hundred residents [S19]. Competitors can be found by zip code, county and region in the Human Services Provider Directory, which DHS refreshes daily [S19].

**What demand means for a new operator.** DHS describes the market as overwhelmingly private pay [S19]. A new residence is therefore competing for residents whose families can fund a monthly fee near the benchmarks above. Mixed-pay demand is the weaker, lower-margin segment in the model (see the financial narrative).

**Medicaid-side demand.** The CHC program serves a large population, but LTSS is not an entitlement and a waitlist forms once participant slots are full (secondary source) [S26]. No CHC waitlist count was found, and no source shows CHC directing members to PCHs or ALRs.

**Referral sources, occupancy, and waitlists.** No statewide PCH/ALR occupancy or vacancy rate, no referral-source mix (hospital discharge, Area Agencies on Aging, placement agencies) and no waitlist figures were found, so none are claimed. The model's 88% default occupancy is an operator planning assumption, not a sourced Pennsylvania figure. Test it with local calls to competing homes before you commit capital.
sections.operations:
**Staffing rules (Chapter 2800, verified).**
- **Administrator:** must be present in the residence an average of 36 hours or more per week in each calendar month [S3]. The related at-least-30-hours-in-business-hours requirement is cited in the DHS fact set from the same chapter. Qualification paths include an RN license plus 1 year of direct care or administrative experience in the prior 10 years [S5]. Before initial employment an administrator must complete a Department-approved orientation, a 100-hour standardized Department-approved administrator training course and a Department-approved competency test with a passing score (§2800.64(a)). Annual training is at least 24 hours (§2800.64(c)), must come from Department-approved sources, and completion must be verified in writing to the ALR Licensing Office [S13]. A DHS training directory dated 03/22/19 listed a 15-hour course; that does not match the 100-hour regulation, so confirm available courses with BHSL [S14].
- **Direct care presence:** a direct care staff person age 21 or older must be in the residence whenever one or more residents are present [S3]. Direct care staff on duty must be awake at all times, so there are no sleep shifts (§2800.58). Modeled as one person on duty 24/7 (730 hours/month) in the 6- and 16-bed models.
- **Service hours:** at least 1 hour/day per mobile resident (2 hours/day for residents with mobility needs), with at least 75% in waking hours [S5].
- **CPR and first aid:** at least one staff person trained in first aid and certified in obstructed airway techniques and CPR must be present at all times for every 35 residents [S3]. The 40-unit models staff two direct care workers at all times, which is an operator staffing choice, not a Chapter 2800 minimum, so base coverage is 1,460 hours/month.
- **Nursing:** the residence must have a licensed nurse available in the building or on call at all times, as an employee or under contract (§2800.60(d)). An LPN under RN supervision, or an RN, must complete or approve the initial assessment, preliminary support plan and final support plan and review the plan quarterly (§2800.227). The models include a contracted nurse/clinical oversight line, sized at $800/month (6 beds), $2,000 (16) and $6,000 (40). These are operator estimates and have not been tested against 24/7 on-call coverage plus assessments; get quotes.
- **Dietitian:** the residence must have a dietitian on staff or under contract for any special dietary needs in a support plan (§2800.60(e)). This cost is not yet priced in the model.
- **Food service, housekeeping, laundry and activities:** three meals plus snacks daily, housekeeping, laundry with weekly linen change, and a daily activities program are mandatory (§2800.220(b), §2800.105(d)), and staffing must cover them (§2800.60(c)). The 6-bed model has no separate line for this work, so its direct care hours are assumed to absorb it.
- **Transportation:** mandatory. The residence must provide or arrange transportation on a regular weekly basis (§2800.171, §2800.220(b)(7)). An own vehicle needs to be wheelchair-accessible, with registration, inspection and insurance records, and the driver must be 18+ and licensed. The $300/month model line is an estimate and may be low.
- **Ratios:** a secondary source claims 1:8 awake and 1:18 asleep. Older summaries say there are no minimum ratios. The conflict is unresolved and no ratio beyond the verified rules is modeled.
- **Direct care training:** direct care staff may not provide unsupervised assisted living services until they complete 18 hours of training and pass the competency test (§2800.65(g)). They must be certified in first aid and CPR before providing care and complete an orientation within 40 scheduled working hours. They need 16 hours of annual training (§2800.65(h)). Dementia training is 4 hours within 30 days of hire and 2 hours annually, in addition (§2800.69). Paid pre-service hours and CPR certification costs are only partly covered by the training line.
- **Criminal history:** checks follow the Older Adult Protective Services Act and its regulations [S15].

**Required systems and costs the model carries.** These are fixed costs in every configuration:
- fire alarm monitoring and inspections ($100–$300/month, estimates), because written fire safety approval is required before licensure [S3]. Approval must be renewed at least every 3 years, with annual fire-safety-expert inspection and drill, furnace and extinguisher inspections;
- eMAR/care documentation software;
- accounting, payroll and legal;
- marketing;
- training and background checks;
- liability insurance (no minimum was found in the rules reviewed, so premiums are estimates);
- DHS license fees;
- transportation.

The 40-unit models also carry a building maintenance contract.

**Physical plant.** New-construction single-resident units must be at least 225 sq ft, and the pre-2011 rule is 160 sq ft [S3]. Each unit also needs its own bathroom with grab bars, an emergency notification system, a lockable door, a telephone jack, an individual thermostat and a window. Central air conditioning is required for new construction. Two wheelchair-accessible common rooms, an AED in each building and a public restroom are required. Startup costs for these are not itemized. The model prices rent per unit, as described below.

**Day-to-day compliance.** The ALR Regulatory Compliance Guide [S12] is the best operating checklist. Expect annual unannounced inspections [S16] and complaint investigations [S19]. Any increase in licensed capacity needs prior DHS approval [S3].
sections.market_conditions:
**Pricing.** The three public benchmarks are $6,100.50/month (Genworth 2024, +10% vs. 2023) [S31], $6,480 (CareScout 2025, secondary citation) [S32] and $5,655 (A Place for Mom) [S33]. Treat the Genworth figure as the central case for an apartment-style residence and the A Place for Mom figure as the closest proxy for a small converted home. Other statewide averages ($4,400 to $5,130) came from sources with unknown methodology and were excluded.

**Wages.** The model uses the Pennsylvania nursing assistant median, $21.44/hr ($44,590/yr), BLS OEWS May 2025 via O*NET [S35]. The national median nursing assistant wage is $42,260/yr [S34], and the national mean in continuing care retirement communities and assisted living facilities was $19.07/hr in May 2024 [S36]. The model also uses the nursing assistant median as a proxy for cooks, housekeepers and activities staff, since those wages were not retrieved. That choice is conservative. Administrator wages were not retrieved at state level. The only reference is the Pittsburgh MSA management occupational group mean of $61.57/hr, about $128,066/yr, May 2025 [S37], which covers all management and is a ceiling. The modeled salaries are operator estimates: $55,000 (6-bed), $70,000 (16) and $95,000 (40).

**Minimum wage.** Pennsylvania's standard minimum wage is $7.25/hr (secondary source) [S38], so every modeled wage is well above it. A $15 bill passed the House [S39] but was blocked in the Senate along party lines [S40]. A change is a risk, not current law. Philadelphia and Pittsburgh cannot set local minimum wages for private employers (secondary) [S41], so no metro has a higher local minimum than the modeled wage.

**Payroll taxes.** PA's unemployment compensation taxable wage base is $10,000 per employee per calendar year [S42]. The 2026 new-employer rate for non-construction employers is 3.822% and experienced-employer rates range from 1.419% to 10.3734% (secondary) [S43]. PCRB workers' compensation loss costs fell 1.22% on April 1, 2026, with an employer assessment factor of 2.18% [S44], but each carrier applies its own loss-cost multiplier [S45]. The model's burden of 9% payroll tax, 4% workers' comp and 5% benefits is partly estimated. See the financial narrative.

**Rent.** The model uses HUD FY2026 Fair Market Rents, which run from October 1, 2025 [S49]. For the Pittsburgh HMFA the 0BR is $1,001 and the 4BR is $1,789. For Philadelphia-Camden-Wilmington the 0BR is $1,397 and the 4BR is $2,423 [S49]. FMRs describe ordinary residential units, not care-use leases. Commercial rent, the purchase price of a building and FY2027 FMRs were not found.

**Metro mismatch.** Wages and price are statewide figures, while rent is Pittsburgh-area. A Philadelphia-area build faces rents roughly 40% higher (studio $1,397 vs. $1,001) [S49]. The effect is quantified in the financial narrative.

**Supply and competition.** No official supply count, market share or competitor data was found, so none are claimed.
sections.financial_narrative:
**How the model is built.** Each configuration takes revenue per resident (price × share of residents), multiplies by licensed capacity and occupancy (88% default; 80% conservative; 95% optimistic, all operator assumptions), and subtracts staffing, payroll burden and opex. Staffing is built from the Chapter 2800 rules [S3][S5]. Presence coverage is 730 hours/month per person on duty (1,460 for the 40-unit models), plus 1 hour/day of service per resident (30.42 hours per resident-month) on top of that, at $21.44/hr [S35]. Adding service time on top of presence is deliberately conservative, since the on-shift person also provides some care and the overlap is unsourced. Rent is fixed and sized to licensed beds, because vacant beds still cost rent. Payroll burden is 9% payroll tax, 4% workers' comp and 5% benefits (18% total). Workers' comp and benefits are operator estimates, and the UC and loss-cost inputs are in the market conditions section. The generator computes break-even itself.

**Results at 88% occupancy.**

| Configuration | Net/month | Margin | Break-even occupancy | First profit month | Cash needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 40-unit, 100% private | $24,335 | 11.3% | 74.7% | 11 | $1,251,234 |
| 16-bed, 100% private | $5,541 | 6.5% | 80.4% | 8 | $391,689 |
| 40-unit, 85% private / 15% SSI-level | $299 | 0.2% | 87.8% | 13 | $1,386,545 |
| 6-bed house, 100% private | -$7,630 | -25.6% | 118.9% | never | $374,089 |
| 16-bed, 75% private / 25% SSI-level | -$10,483 | -15.0% | 107.1% | never | $751,768 |

A break-even occupancy above 100% means the configuration cannot reach break-even even when full. The default configuration is the 40-unit private-pay residence.

**Why the 6-bed house loses.** At $5,655/month [S33], 5.3 residents bring in about $29,900/month. The 24/7 coverage line alone costs about $18,500/month with burden, before service time, a paid administrator, rent and fixed overhead. Only an owner who personally fills the care shifts and pays themselves little changes this. That is a labor choice, not a model result, and it is not shown.

**Unit economics.** At the Genworth price of $6,100.50, each additional private-pay resident adds roughly $4,570/month after about $1,535 of variable cost. That figure combines per-resident opex of $765 with roughly $770 for the rule-based service time including burden. It is my arithmetic from the model lines. Both the 16- and 40-bed profits come almost entirely from filling the building. Moving from 88% to 95% occupancy adds roughly $12,800/month in the 40-unit model and roughly $5,100 in the 16-bed model.

**Occupancy sensitivity (approximate, by arithmetic from the model).** The 40-unit private model nets about $9,700/month at 80% occupancy and about $37,000 at 95%. The 16-bed private model is about break-even to slightly negative (about -$300) at 80% and about $10,650 at 95%. A single vacancy is about 6% of a 16-bed census.

**Price sensitivity.** At the lower A Place for Mom price ($5,655), the 40-unit model falls to roughly $8,650/month and the 16-bed model becomes a loss of roughly $730/month. At the CareScout 2025 figure ($6,480), the 40-unit model rises to roughly $37,700 and the 16-bed model to roughly $10,900. Genworth and CareScout measure private one-bedrooms in assisted living communities, so confirm what your local competitors actually charge.

**Why SSI-level residents erase the margin.** An SSI-level resident contributes $1,548.30/month [S21][S23], almost exactly the roughly $1,535 of variable cost that resident causes, so each one adds about nothing toward rent and staff. Replacing a $6,100.50 private-pay resident with one costs about $4,552/month. That explains the swing in the 40-unit model, from $24,335 to $299 with 15% SSI-level residents, and in the 16-bed model, which loses $10,483 at a 25% mix. The $85 allowance and the payment mechanics are secondary-sourced, and no CHC revenue is modeled.

**Service-hour sensitivity.** If residents need the 2 hours/day tier [S5], the model notes put the added direct care cost at about $12,000/month for the 16-bed (at 88% occupancy, with burden) and about $27,000/month for the 40-unit. Either increase exceeds the modeled profit at default occupancy. Resident acuity and assessment mix, not just price, decide the result.

**Wage sensitivity.** Each $1/hour change in the modeled wage moves the result by roughly $4,000/month in the 40-unit model, $1,700 in the 16-bed and $1,050 in the 6-bed, including burden. The modeled $21.44 is a statewide median [S35], above the $19.07 national assisted-living industry mean [S36]. The model's use of that median for cooks and housekeepers is conservative.

**Administrator cost.** The administrator salaries are estimates. At the Pittsburgh management group mean of $61.57/hr [S37], the results would fall by about $7,200 (6-bed), $5,700 (16-bed) and $3,250 (40-unit) per month, per the model notes.

**Geography sensitivity.** Rent uses Pittsburgh-area HUD FMRs. Replacing the studio FMR with the Philadelphia-area $1,397 [S49], and keeping the 35% common-area uplift, adds roughly $21,400/month to the 40-unit model and $8,550 to the 16-bed model. That drops the 40-unit net to roughly $2,950 and turns the 16-bed into roughly a $3,000 monthly loss, before any price premium Philadelphia might support. No Philadelphia-specific price was found.

**What the model leaves out.** Rent is a floor. It uses FMRs plus a 35% common-area allowance and excludes purchase, construction or tenant-improvement debt. Insurance premiums, the nurse oversight lines and most other operating costs are estimates. The $1.25 million for the 40-unit residence is cash needed per the model, and the model finds first profit in month 11 on a ramp of 4 residents at start plus 3 per month. No sourced reserve minimum applies.
sections.risks:
**Regulatory risk.**
- The per-bed fee was adjusted by a 2018 Pennsylvania Bulletin notice and can rise again [S5]. The $75 base used in the model is likely stale and the current amount is unverified.
- The initial fee timing is unresolved between the regulation and DHS notices [S6][S7][S8].
- No rule-stated processing time exists, so opening dates are uncertain.
- The Pa. Code is current only through the date on the site [S51]. Rulemaking after that date, and waiver-of-regulation requests [S50], could change requirements.
- Administrator qualification is a 100-hour course plus orientation and a competency test, with 24 hours of annual training. Direct care staff need 18 hours before unsupervised work and 16 hours annually, plus dementia training. The model's training lines are estimates and may be too low.
- Required costs not fully priced: a dietitian contract, an accessible vehicle and driver labor for mandatory transportation, and unit-level plant upgrades. Actual profit will be lower than modeled.
- The 40-unit staffing of two direct care workers at all times is an operator choice; staff must be awake at all times, so there is no sleep-shift discount.
- Operating without a license triggers a $500 penalty plus $20 per resident per day after 14 days (§2800.262(g)) [S3].
- Many requirements cannot be waived (staff training, fire safety, assessment/support plans, contracts, resident rights), so a waiver cannot fix a shortfall there.

**Licensing-side unknowns.** Zoning, certificate-of-occupancy and State Fire Marshal approval requirements, process and fees were not verified [S12]. Written fire safety approval must come before the license [S3], and the building work behind it is the biggest unmodeled variable in the startup budget. No insurance or bond minimum was found. Workers' compensation is mandatory for employers with employees; the class code and the 4% rate are unverified and may be low for direct-care labor.

**Market risk.**
- Private-pay benchmarks conflict ($5,655, $6,100.50, $6,480) [S31][S32][S33] and none measures small homes.
- No Pennsylvania occupancy data was found, so 88% is an assumption.
- The 16-bed model needs about 80.4% occupancy and the 40-unit about 74.7%. A slow ramp, or vacancies in a small census, erodes that margin quickly.

**Payer-mix risk.** SSI-level residents bring in about the same as their variable cost. At 15% of a 40-unit census the margin falls to 0.2%, and at 25% of a 16-bed census the model loses $10,483/month. Whether the state supplement applies to ALR residents is unverified. Medicaid and CHC are not a reliable offset: DHS says PCH and ALR charges are typically not covered by Medicaid [S19], and the CHC re-procurement is in a stay with plans continuing until further notice [S52].

**Labor risk.** Wages are 18% higher once burden is added and are the largest cost. The $15 minimum wage bill is not law [S39][S40], but a statewide increase would push up entry-level wages. Direct care turnover and agency substitutes are not modeled. A higher administrator salary would reduce profit as shown in the financial narrative.

**Rent and capital risk.** FMR is a floor, and the 40-unit model excludes the cost of buying or building the facility. A Philadelphia-area site takes the 40-unit model to roughly break-even and the 16-bed model into a loss. FY2027 FMRs were not verified.

**Acuity risk.** If residents need mobility help (2 hours/day) [S5], direct care costs rise by an amount larger than the modeled profit in the 16- and 40-bed models.

**Data quality.** Most quotes in this bundle came from search-result excerpts, not full-page fetches. LLC fees, the minimum wage and the UC new-employer rate are secondary-sourced. The CareScout, A Place for Mom and Pittsburgh management wage figures could not be re-verified from primary pages. Re-verify before relying on them. BHSL's headquarters address and phone also conflict across DHS pages.
sections.recommendations:
**1. Do not open a small house staffed by paid labor.** The 6-bed private-pay model loses $7,630/month and cannot break even even when full. Consider this size only if the owner personally provides the 24/7 coverage and takes little pay, and treat that as a lifestyle business, not the modeled one. Also check whether a PCH license under Chapter 2600 fits a small home better. That chapter's staffing and plant rules were not researched here.

**2. Lead with the 40-unit private-pay residence if you have the capital and a strong referral base.** It is the best result in the model: $24,335/month at 88% occupancy, 74.7% break-even, first profit in month 11. It also needs about $1.25 million, with no building purchase included. Secure the site first, because rent is the major swing factor.

**3. The 16-bed private-pay residence is a lower-capital but thin option.** It nets $5,541/month, needs 80.4% occupancy, and needs about $392,000. It works only at or near the Genworth or CareScout price level, in a Pittsburgh-rent market, with a sourced local price at least that high. At the A Place for Mom price it loses money.

**4. Keep SSI-level residents to a small, deliberate share.** At roughly $1,548.30/month an SSI-level resident covers about only their own variable cost. If your mission includes serving them, price the rest of the building for it and cap the share. Do not assume Medicaid or CHC will fill the gap.

**5. Before spending money, confirm with BHSL:**
- when the initial fee is paid and whether renewal is annual;
- the current per-bed amount;
- the nurse coverage requirement;
- the CPR/first-aid reading for 40 residents;
- current training hours.

Call the Operator Support Hotline at (866) 503-3926 [S17], and confirm the BHSL headquarters address.

**6. Run the local numbers.** Replace the operator estimates (rent, insurance, nurse, administrator, workers' comp) with quotes. Call competitors from the Human Services Provider Directory to set a local price and test the 88% occupancy assumption [S19]. If your site is in the Philadelphia area, rerun the model at local rent. The Pittsburgh-based figures will not hold.

**7. Protect the ramp.** The 40-unit model reaches profit only after about 11 months. Plan referral relationships, a marketing budget and cash for a ramp slower than the model's 3 admissions a month, and keep a reserve for the 80% occupancy case.

**8. Watch the staffing economics.** Each $1/hr wage change moves the 40-unit result by about $4,000/month. Admit residents who need only the 1 hour/day tier where your license and assessments allow, and price additional care tiers to cover the 2 hour/day case rather than absorbing it.

**9. Treat Medicaid as optional upside to research, not a plan.** If you want to serve CHC participants, talk to the CHC managed care plans and OLTL about whether any payment applies in an ALR or PCH setting, and check whether the $750 federal enrollment fee [S30] applies. EVV rules apply to in-home personal care visits [S29]. None of this is modeled.

checklist.task: Choose the license type: Assisted Living Residence (ALR, Ch. 2800) or Personal Care Home (PCH, Ch. 2600)
checklist.instructions: Both license types cover four or more adults who are not relatives of the operator, served for more than 24 hours. They sit under separate chapters, and Ch. 2800 expressly does not apply to personal care homes. This bundle's financial model and checklist are built on the ALR rules. The PCH rules in Ch. 2600 were not researched in detail. If you choose PCH, read Ch. 2600 in full and rebuild the staffing plan before committing.

checklist.task: Confirm the regulator and open a line with the licensing bureau
checklist.instructions: DHS's Office of Long-Term Living, through the Bureau of Human Services Licensing (BHSL), licenses both PCHs and ALRs. Call the BHSL Operator Support Hotline at (866) 503-3926 with licensing-process questions. BHSL headquarters is 717-783-3670 / ra-pwarlheadquarters@pa.gov. A DHS field-office page lists a different address and phone, so confirm the right contact before mailing anything. Free.

checklist.task: Read Chapter 2800 in full and check that your copy is current
checklist.instructions: Use the official Pa. Code text. The site states it is current through 56 Pa.B. 5370 (Aug. 8, 2026), so check the Pennsylvania Bulletin for amendments after that date. No pending 2026 rulemaking on Ch. 2600 or 2800 was found in this research. Allow 1–2 days to read.

checklist.task: Study the DHS ALR Regulatory Compliance Guide
checklist.instructions: The guide shows how inspectors read each Ch. 2800 requirement, including the certificate-of-occupancy check. Use it as the master list for your policies, building and staffing, and keep it for mock inspections later. Free.

checklist.task: Review the ALR Prelicensure Checklist and the Policy Review List
checklist.instructions: These are the two DHS BHSL documents that define what you file before the initial inspection. Download the current versions from the DHS PCH & ALR Licensing page (the checklist is dated 1/14/2025). Build your application calendar around them.
checklist.cite: ALR Prelicensure Checklist; 2800 ALR Policy Review List

checklist.task: Pick your size and payer model from the Pro Forma before you spend money
checklist.instructions: In the model, the 40-unit private-pay residence is the only configuration that is clearly profitable at the default 88% occupancy. The 16-bed private-pay residence is marginal. The 6-bed home and the 16-bed home with SSI-level residents lose money at the sourced prices. The 40-unit home with SSI-level residents is about break-even. Occupancy, price and the nursing-assistant wage are the swing factors. Re-run the Pro Forma with your local rent, wages and price. Homes may be licensed for as few as four residents or as many as several hundred.
checklist.cite: Pro Forma P&L; DHS PCH/ALR overview

checklist.task: Survey the local market in the Human Services Provider Directory
checklist.instructions: Search licensed PCHs and ALRs by zip code, county and region. The directory is refreshed daily. Note nearby capacity and building types, then call a few to check pricing. No official statewide occupancy figures or competitor data exist in the sources reviewed, so local calls are your only occupancy evidence.

checklist.task: Form the legal entity and obtain an EIN
checklist.instructions: File a Certificate of Organization with the PA Department of State. The reported LLC fee is $125 one-time (secondary source, so verify against the Department of State fee schedule). A foreign LLC registers for $250. Pennsylvania has no LLC franchise tax; members pay the flat 3.07% personal income tax on pass-through income. The licensee name on the DHS application should match the entity exactly. Get a free EIN from the IRS, usually the same day, for payroll and banking.
checklist.cite: PA Dept. of State; IRS Form SS-4

checklist.task: Calendar the LLC annual report
checklist.instructions: Pennsylvania LLCs file a $7 annual report each year under Act 122 of 2022. Most sources give September 30 as the due date and one source conflicts, so confirm on the Department of State site.

checklist.task: Open the business bank account and set up a separate funding reserve
checklist.instructions: Use the Pro Forma's cash-needed and ramp-up deficit figures to size your reserve. No minimum cash reserve was found in the Ch. 2800 sources reviewed, so lenders and landlords will set the real requirement. Allow 3–6 months of expenses for ramp-up.

checklist.task: Check municipal business registration and local earned-income / wage tax
checklist.instructions: Contact the municipality (and school district) where the residence will sit. Local business, earned income and wage tax obligations were not verified. Philadelphia, for example, has its own wage tax (3.74% for residents, secondary source). Allow 1–2 weeks.

checklist.task: Screen buildings against the physical-plant rules before you sign anything
checklist.instructions: In new construction after January 18, 2011, a single-resident living unit must have at least 225 sq ft of floor space. Pre-2011 facilities fall under the 160 sq ft rule. Use the Ch. 2800 text and the compliance guide to check bathrooms, exits and common space.

checklist.task: Confirm zoning with the municipality in writing
checklist.instructions: Get a written zoning determination for the use before you commit to the site. No official DHS or municipal zoning rule was retrieved in this research. A secondary source lists proof of zoning approval among application materials, but this is not confirmed against DHS. Ask BHSL whether it wants zoning evidence in the packet. Fees and timing vary by municipality.
checklist.cite: Local zoning ordinance; DHS Policy Review List

checklist.task: Verify the certificate of occupancy and whether the use change needs a new or modified one
checklist.instructions: Inspectors verify that the residence has a new or modified certificate of occupancy before the building's use changes. Ask the municipal code office what is needed for assisted living use in this building. Costs and timelines vary by municipality and were not verified.

checklist.task: Plan for written fire safety approval before licensure
checklist.instructions: A written fire safety approval is required before an ALR license is issued. The State Fire Marshal floor-plan approval process and fees were not verified from official sources, so ask BHSL which approving authority applies to your building and locality. Budget for alarm, smoke detection and any sprinkler work (operator estimates in the Pro Forma).

checklist.task: Prepare a floor plan of every level showing all internal and external exits
checklist.instructions: The pre-licensure package must include a layout of all floors and levels that clearly indicates every internal and external exit path and exit door. Have an architect or designer draw it to scale and match the room count to the capacity you want licensed.

checklist.task: Decide your licensed capacity with growth in mind
checklist.instructions: Capacity is fixed on the license. An increase must be requested from DHS and other applicable authorities and approved before additional residents are admitted. If you may add units later, plan for that now when you pick the building.

checklist.task: Negotiate the lease or purchase with licensing and zoning contingencies
checklist.instructions: Make the lease contingent on DHS licensure, zoning approval and certificate of occupancy. HUD FY2026 Fair Market Rents are a residential floor, not a commercial care-use rent: Pittsburgh HMFA studio is $1,001 and 4BR $1,789, and Philadelphia MSA studio is $1,397 and 4BR $2,423. FY2027 figures (effective Oct 1, 2026) were not verified. Vacant units still cost rent.

checklist.task: Get contractor quotes for fire alarm, extinguishers, accessibility and unit upgrades
checklist.instructions: Start from the fire safety approval requirement and the 225 / 160 sq ft unit rule. All Pro Forma building costs are operator estimates; replace them with written quotes. Allow 2–4 weeks for quotes.

checklist.task: Download the current DHS application packet
checklist.instructions: Use the DHS Application for License page for the current form and instructions. The current ALR form, any online submission portal and the 2026 DHS fee letter were not verified, so use the live page, not older copies. A civil rights form goes in the packet.

checklist.task: File the pre-licensure documents with BHSL headquarters before the initial inspection
checklist.instructions: The documentation package goes to the BHSL headquarters office before the initial inspection is scheduled. Work through the Prelicensure Checklist line by line and keep copies of everything submitted.

checklist.task: Complete the Policy Review List for a new ALR
checklist.instructions: The list requires administrator education/training documentation and criminal history checks for the owner/operator, among other items. Write your policies to the Ch. 2800 requirements, using the compliance guide for what inspectors look for.

checklist.task: Obtain criminal history checks for owners and operators
checklist.instructions: Checks follow the Older Adult Protective Services Act and its regulations (6 Pa. Code Ch. 15). Owners or operators who are not Pennsylvania residents and who will work in the residence must also provide an FBI criminal history background check. Start early. Fees and turnaround were not verified.
checklist.cite: Older Adult Protective Services Act; 6 Pa. Code Ch. 15

checklist.task: Understand the ALR fees you will pay
checklist.instructions: The ALR license application or renewal fee is a flat $300. A per-bed fee also applies: $75 per bed base, which DHS may adjust annually up to the Consumer Price Index. The current adjusted per-bed amount was not verified, so ask BHSL. Base cost is $750 at 6 beds, $1,500 at 16 beds and $3,300 at 40 beds.

checklist.task: Confirm exactly when the initial fee is due and how to pay
checklist.instructions: A relay of a DHS notice says a new application is mailed with the supporting documents and the fee as a check or money order payable to DHS. The regulation text ties the fees to issuing or renewing the license, which suggests payment after DHS finds the residence compliant. These two readings conflict, so confirm with BHSL before sending money. For renewals, DHS requires the application fee with the renewal application and the ALR per-bed fee before the renewal certificate issues.
checklist.cite: 55 Pa. Code §2800.11; DHS Application for License

checklist.task: Do not admit or hold out residents before the license is issued
checklist.instructions: DHS must inspect a new ALR and find it compliant before it can open, operate or admit residents. Operating without a license carries a $500 penalty, plus $20 per resident per day if you do not file an application within 14 days.

checklist.task: Plan the licensing timeline without relying on a published processing time
checklist.instructions: No rule-stated days-to-license was found. Ask the BHSL hotline for current review and inspection scheduling times, and build a buffer into your lease start date and pre-opening payroll.

checklist.task: If a rule cannot be met, check the waiver-of-regulation process
checklist.instructions: DHS posts ALR waiver-of-regulation requests for a 30-day public comment period. Review the DHS PCH & ALR Licensing page for current requests and the procedure. The contents of open requests were not retrieved.

checklist.task: If you choose a PCH instead, price the PCH fee and confirm its tiers
checklist.instructions: Ch. 2600 bases the PCH application fee on beds: $15 (0–20 beds), $20 (21–50), $30 (51–100), $50 (101+) per the regulation as reproduced by Cornell LII. DHS's own application page lists a different smallest tier (4–20 beds), so confirm with BHSL. DHS reinspects a newly licensed PCH within 3 months of initial licensure.

checklist.task: Appoint a qualified administrator
checklist.instructions: One qualifying path is an RN license from the Department of State plus 1 year, in the prior 10 years, of direct care or administrative experience in a health care or human services field. Other paths include LPN and nursing home administrator licenses. The full list of alternatives and any age or shared-administrator conditions were not verified, so read the qualification section of Ch. 2800 and the compliance guide.

checklist.task: Schedule the administrator for 36+ hours a week on site
checklist.instructions: The administrator must be present in the residence an average of 36 hours or more per week in each calendar month, with at least 30 of those hours during business hours. If you are the owner-administrator, that time is your own pay line in the Pro Forma.

checklist.task: Complete administrator training and orientation from DHS-approved sources
checklist.instructions: Annual administrator training must come from Department-approved sources, and completion must be verified in writing to the ALR Licensing Office. The DHS directory (dated 3/22/2019) lists a 15-hour assisted living administrator training course, but the current hours and the full §2800.64 breakdown were not verified. Course prices are operator estimates.

checklist.task: Build the 24/7 schedule around the staff-presence rule
checklist.instructions: At all times one or more residents are present, a direct care staff person age 21 or older must be present in the residence. The Pro Forma models 730 hours a month for one person, and 1,460 hours for the 40-unit residence.

checklist.task: Budget the required direct care time per resident
checklist.instructions: Direct care staff must be available to provide at least 1 hour per day of assisted living services to each mobile resident, and 2 hours per day for residents with mobility needs. At least 75% of the service hours must fall during waking hours. Residents needing more help raise your labor cost sharply, so screen admissions against your staffing.
checklist.cite: 55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800 (assisted living service hours)

checklist.task: Keep first-aid / CPR coverage on site at all times
checklist.instructions: For every 35 residents there must be at least one staff person trained in first aid and certified in obstructed airway techniques and CPR present in the residence at all times. At 40 residents, the Pro Forma reads this as two trained staff. Confirm that interpretation with BHSL.

checklist.task: Confirm the current nursing coverage requirement with BHSL
checklist.instructions: A 2015 federal compendium says a registered nurse must be available in the building or on call at all times. Later summaries describe a licensed nurse requirement, and the current official requirement was not confirmed. Ask BHSL, then contract with a nurse. The Pro Forma carries a contracted nurse line as an operator estimate.

checklist.task: Confirm current direct care staff training requirements before hiring
checklist.instructions: Only dated sources were found: a 2015 compendium (18 hours of training with a demonstration of job duties before unsupervised work) and a 2019 summary (16 hours annual). Check the current Ch. 2800 training section and the compliance guide, and build the hours into onboarding.
checklist.cite: HHS ASPE Compendium 2015 (PA); 55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800

checklist.task: Run criminal history checks on every staff member before they work with residents
checklist.instructions: Checks must be done in accordance with the Older Adult Protective Services Act and its regulations (6 Pa. Code Ch. 15). Keep the results in each personnel file. Costs and turnaround were not verified.

checklist.task: Set wages from PA data and re-check them locally
checklist.instructions: The Pro Forma uses the PA nursing assistant median of $21.44/hr ($44,590/yr), BLS OEWS May 2025 via O*NET. The state minimum wage is $7.25/hr. A $15 bill passed the House but is not enacted, and Philadelphia and Pittsburgh cannot set higher local minimums for private employers (secondary source). Wages for cooks, housekeepers and RNs were not retrieved, so check local job postings.
checklist.cite: BLS OEWS May 2025; PA minimum wage

checklist.task: Benchmark the administrator salary
checklist.instructions: Administrator-specific PA wage data was not retrieved. The Pittsburgh MSA management group mean is $61.57/hr (about $128,066/yr), BLS May 2025. This covers all management occupations, so treat it as a ceiling and check local postings for ALR administrators.
checklist.cite: BLS Occupational Employment and Wages, Pittsburgh, May 2025

checklist.task: Hire and train staff before the initial inspection
checklist.instructions: DHS inspects before you can open or admit residents, so staff and the administrator should be in place and trained for that visit. Budget pre-opening payroll; the Pro Forma carries it as an operator estimate.

checklist.task: Draft the resident-residence contract
checklist.instructions: The contract must identify the assisted living services in the core service package the resident is purchasing and the total price for those services. Have a Pennsylvania attorney review it against Ch. 2800 and the compliance guide before the first admission.

checklist.task: Set your private-pay price from local comparables
checklist.instructions: Public benchmarks differ: Genworth 2024 PA median $73,206/yr (about $6,100/mo), CareScout 2025 via a secondary guide $6,480/mo, and A Place for Mom $5,655/mo. Genworth and CareScout measure a private one-bedroom in an assisted living community, so they may overstate revenue for a small converted house. Call nearby residences before setting a rate.

checklist.task: Write the policies listed on the DHS Policy Review List
checklist.instructions: Draft them against the Ch. 2800 text and the compliance guide. DHS reviews them as part of a new-residence application, so keep a controlled copy for the inspector.

checklist.task: Decide whether you will accept SSI-level residents, and at what payment
checklist.instructions: DHS says PCH and ALR rates are set by the facility. The 2026 SSI plus state supplement is $1,633.30/month for a personal care boarding home (SSA). A secondary source states the SSI-level payment is that amount minus an $85 personal needs allowance (§2600.25a), or $1,548.30/month. The allowance and the mechanics were not verified from DHS. The model shows that a 25% SSI share at 16 beds loses money and that 15% at 40 units is about break-even.

checklist.task: Do not plan on Medicaid or Community HealthChoices revenue for residence charges
checklist.instructions: DHS states PCHs and ALRs are typically not covered by Medicaid and that the facility sets its rates. A secondary source reports Pennsylvania has no assisted-living Medicaid waiver. Community HealthChoices (CHC) is OLTL's Medicaid managed long-term services and supports program, not a licensing pathway. Some residents also receive Home and Community-Based Services. The model includes no CHC revenue.
checklist.cite: DHS Personal Care Homes & Assisted Living Residences page

checklist.task: If you later contract for Medicaid-funded services, check enrollment, EVV and fees first
checklist.instructions: DHS requires EVV for Medicaid-funded personal care or home health services that require an in-home visit. The CY2026 federal enrollment application fee is $750 for institutional providers (secondary source), and whether it applies to a PCH or ALR operator was not confirmed. Also check CHC status: OLTL's re-procurement is in a stay, and current MCOs continue until further notice (April 2026).

checklist.task: Check the OLTL HCBS fee schedules if you add any Medicaid-funded services
checklist.instructions: DHS lists OLTL HCBS rate files dated January 1 and July 1, 2026, but the amounts were not retrieved for this bundle. Rates are set by DHS through an actuarial process with public comment and billed in quarter-hour units. Download the current files from DHS rather than relying on this bundle.

checklist.task: Set up an eMAR / care documentation system and written resident records
checklist.instructions: Get quotes from several vendors; the Pro Forma carries this as an operator estimate. No Medicaid revenue is modeled, so no EVV cost is included.

checklist.task: Build referral relationships and your marketing plan
checklist.instructions: Referral-source data for PA PCH/ALR admissions was not found, so treat all referral assumptions as your own estimates. Pennsylvania had more than 2.5 million residents aged 65+ in the 2020 Census (Dept. of Aging); later estimates differ. Use the Provider Directory to see where your competition sits.

checklist.task: Register as an employer for Pennsylvania unemployment compensation (UC)
checklist.instructions: The UC taxable wage base is $10,000 per employee per calendar year (L&I Yearly Tax Highlights). The 2026 new-employer rate for non-construction employers is 3.822%, and experienced-employer rates range from 1.419% to 10.3734% (secondary source). Confirm your assigned rate with L&I.
checklist.cite: PA Dept. of Labor & Industry, Yearly Tax Highlights

checklist.task: Set up payroll withholding and local wage taxes
checklist.instructions: Pennsylvania withholds a flat 3.07% personal income tax on wages. Local earned income or wage taxes also apply; the Philadelphia resident wage tax is 3.74% (secondary source). Municipal rates in other areas and Pittsburgh's local wage tax were not verified. Use a payroll provider.
checklist.cite: PA personal income tax; local EIT

checklist.task: Obtain workers' compensation and confirm requirements for your operation
checklist.instructions: Whether coverage is mandatory for this operator type, and the PCRB class code for assisted living, were not verified. PCRB advisory loss costs fell 1.22% effective April 1, 2026, but each carrier applies its own loss-cost multiplier, so get several quotes. The Pro Forma uses a 4% operator estimate.

checklist.task: Buy general and professional liability insurance
checklist.instructions: No insurance or bond minimum for ALR or PCH licensure was found in the sources reviewed. Landlords, lenders and referral partners usually require coverage. Get quotes from carriers that write assisted living, and ask BHSL whether it needs a certificate. The Pro Forma carries premium as an operator estimate.

checklist.task: Add commercial auto and property coverage if you transport residents or own the building
checklist.instructions: Transportation is optional in the model (operator estimate). If residents ride in a business vehicle, carry commercial auto coverage. Price it with your agent.

checklist.task: Engage an accountant for entity tax and payroll
checklist.instructions: Pennsylvania has no LLC franchise tax, and members pay 3.07% on pass-through income (secondary source). Confirm your entity classification and any local business taxes. Budget accounting and legal as operator estimates.
checklist.cite: Pennsylvania LLC Annual Report and Taxes (2026)

checklist.task: Pass the pre-licensure inspection
checklist.instructions: Before the residence is initially licensed and permitted to open, operate or admit residents, DHS inspects it. Run an internal mock inspection first, using the compliance guide as the checklist, with the building, staff, records and policies in place.

checklist.task: Pay the licensing fees at the time BHSL directs and receive the license
checklist.instructions: The fees ($300 plus the per-bed fee) are conditions of issuing the license. Follow BHSL's written instruction on when and how to pay, and keep proof of payment. Do not admit anyone until the license is in hand.

checklist.task: Verify the license shows the correct entity, address and capacity
checklist.instructions: Check the issued license for the exact licensee name, site address and licensed capacity. Fix errors with BHSL right away, because capacity increases need prior DHS approval.

checklist.task: Admit residents on a planned ramp
checklist.instructions: The Pro Forma assumes 1 admission per month for the 6-bed home, 2 per month for 16 beds and 3 per month for 40 units. Verify against your referral pipeline. The model shows first profit in month 8 for the 16-bed private-pay residence and month 11 for the 40-unit private-pay residence.

checklist.task: Prepare for the reinspection within 3 months of initial licensure
checklist.instructions: DHS reinspects newly licensed residences within 3 months of the date of initial licensure. Treat it as a second full inspection: staffing records, training, contracts, and resident records should all be complete.

checklist.task: Expect an annual unannounced inspection and complaint investigations
checklist.instructions: The statute requires at least one annual onsite unannounced inspection of each PCH and ALR, and DHS investigates complaints and unusual incidents. Keep records inspection-ready every day.

checklist.task: Renew the license on time with the renewal application and fees
checklist.instructions: DHS requires the application fee with the renewal application. The ALR per-bed fee is due before the renewal certificate issues. Check the current per-bed amount, since DHS may adjust it annually up to CPI. Set a calendar reminder well before the renewal date.

checklist.task: Complete and document annual administrator training
checklist.instructions: Training must come from Department-approved sources, with written verification to the ALR Licensing Office. Keep the certificates in the administrator's file.

checklist.task: Re-audit the schedule against the 1 hr/day and 2 hrs/day service-time rules
checklist.instructions: Each time a resident's mobility needs change, recheck whether you now owe 2 hours per day for that resident and whether at least 75% of service hours fall in waking hours. In the model, 2 hrs/day roughly doubles that labor line.
checklist.cite: 55 Pa. Code Ch. 2800 (assisted living service hours)

checklist.task: Monitor rule changes and DHS licensing notices
checklist.instructions: Check the Pennsylvania Bulletin and the DHS PCH & ALR Licensing page (What's New) for rule changes, waiver-of-regulation notices and statistical reports. Re-run the Pro Forma when rent, wage or price assumptions change.
checklist.cite: Pennsylvania Code & Bulletin; DHS PCH & ALR Licensing page

checklist.task: Track the state minimum wage and your own wage competitiveness
checklist.instructions: The state minimum wage is $7.25/hr. A $15 bill passed the House and the Senate has not acted on it, so it is not law. Because your 24/7 coverage runs at about $21/hr, local competition matters more than the state floor. Review wages at least once a year.

checklist.task: File the annual LLC report and renew local registrations
checklist.instructions: The $7 annual report is due each September 30 per most sources. Renew any municipal business registration and keep payroll tax filings current.

checklist.task: Review your price against the market every year
checklist.instructions: Re-check Genworth/CareScout, local competitors and the Provider Directory. Remember that Genworth reported PA assisted living up 10% versus 2023, but that figure is for a private one-bedroom in an AL community. Update contracts for new residents; contracts must state the total price for the core service package.
